The Capital Asset Pricing Model and the theory of risk and return.
Forwards, futures, options, and swaps — the core derivative instruments and how they are priced and used.
The EMH, its forms, and the debate over the existence of alpha. Notes in progress.

Why quantitative finance, what this site covers, and how to use the roadmap.

From a single artificial neuron to deep nets — layers and the forward pass, activation functions, loss functions, backpropagation, optimizers (SGD → Adam), weight initialization, and CNNs/RNNs — with runnable examples and a quant framing.
Decision trees, random forests, boosting (AdaBoost / Gradient Boosting / XGBoost) and support vector machines — how each works, when to reach for it, and runnable examples with a quant framing.

What machine learning actually is — AI vs ML vs DL vs data science, every type of learning, instance- vs model-based learning, the geometry of the hyperplane, and the end-to-end project lifecycle, framed for a quant.

Where the whole ML toolkit meets markets — why finance breaks the usual assumptions, financial feature engineering and labeling, the traps that wreck backtests (leakage, overfitting, survivorship, costs), and honest walk-forward evaluation, with a runnable example.

The bias-variance tradeoff, train/validation/test discipline, every kind of cross-validation, regression and classification metrics (and why accuracy lies), plus the leakage traps that make financial validation different.

Turning text into numbers a model can use — tokenization, stemming/lemmatization, stopwords, POS/NER, Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, and Word2Vec embeddings — ending in a runnable sentiment classifier, with a quant framing on news and filings.

Machine learning as a quant's toolkit — a complete, hands-on path from fundamentals to market applications, where every page pairs the core method with a runnable in-browser example and a real quant use.

The supervised workhorses — linear and polynomial regression, L1/L2/ElasticNet regularization, logistic regression, k-Nearest Neighbors, and Naive Bayes — how each learns, when to use it, and runnable examples.
Policy search, Q-learning, and RL for trading. Notes in progress.

Finding structure without labels — PCA and dimensionality reduction, K-Means / hierarchical / DBSCAN clustering, the silhouette score, and anomaly detection with Isolation Forest and LOF, with runnable examples and a quant framing.

Independent vs dependent events, conditional probability, and the multiplication rule for 'and' — plus the one-line step to Bayes' theorem — with runnable examples and why dependence is the heart of risk.

The right-skewed, positive-only distribution whose logarithm is normal. If Y = ln(X) is normal then X is log-normal. Interactive density, a 3D view of skew growing with σ, the real-world examples (wealth, salaries), and why stock prices are modeled log-normal.

The symmetric bell — the workhorse continuous distribution. Its PDF, the parameters μ and σ², mean = median = mode, the 68–95–99.7 empirical rule, an interactive explorer, a 3D joint bell, and why quants both rely on it and distrust its thin tails.
The standard normal N(0,1) and the z-score (x−μ)/σ that maps any normal onto it. Worked from the lecture's own examples, plus standardization — putting Age, Weight, Salary on one scale for ML models.

The flat distribution where every outcome is equally likely — continuous (a PDF, 1/(b−a)) and discrete (a PMF, 1/n). Worked candy-sales and fair-die examples, an interactive area lab, mean/median/variance, and the quant reading (Monte Carlo, no-view priors).
The simplest discrete distribution — one trial, two outcomes. Its PMF p^k(1-p)^(1-k), mean p, and variance pq, with an interactive bar chart and the quant reading of a single binary bet.

Bernoulli, run n times — the number of successes in n independent yes/no trials. Its PMF nCk p^k q^(n-k), mean np, variance npq, with an interactive bar chart, a 3D view of the PMF growing with n, and the two lecture worked examples.

The distribution of counts — how many events occur in a fixed interval at a constant average rate λ. PMF e^(−λ)λ^x/x!, the signature mean = variance = λ, an interactive PMF, a 3D view, and the quant reading (arrivals, jumps, rare events).

The three functions that describe any distribution — the probability mass function for discrete variables, the probability density function for continuous ones, and the cumulative distribution function that connects them. Density is the slope of the CDF.
documents.s: The Relationship Between PMF, PDF and CDF

documents.t: A map of the named distributions — which are discrete (PMF) and which are continuous (PDF), and how the columns of a real dataset each pick their own distribution.

The named power-law distribution behind the 80–20 rule. Pareto Type I PDF, the tail index α, an interactive density and 3D tail view, the transforms back to normal, and why actuaries and risk managers model large losses with it.

The 80–20 rule made precise — a functional relationship where one quantity varies as a power of another, producing a long tail where a few outcomes dominate. Log-log straight lines, the transform back to normal, and why finance lives here.

The theorem that makes statistics work — the sampling distribution of the mean is normal, N(μ, σ/√n), no matter what the population looks like, once n is large enough. An interactive demo, a 3D view of the standard error, and why quants can trust an average.

Using an observed statistic to stand in for an unknown population parameter — point estimates (a single value) versus interval estimates (a range, the confidence interval). Built on the CLT's standard error, with the quant reading that every number is an estimate with error.
Why the average of many independent draws converges to the true mean — the weak and strong laws, how it differs from the CLT, and why it underwrites Monte Carlo and every long-run edge.

Priors, likelihoods, and posteriors — conjugate priors, the posterior predictive, grid/quadratic approximation and MCMC, credible intervals (HPDI) and the ROPE decision — with an interactive prior-to-posterior lab.

Correlation is not causation — and directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are the tool that tells you which variables to control for, which to leave alone, and when a regression coefficient can be read as an effect.

Covariance gets the direction of a relationship right but leaves its strength uninterpretable — the magnitude is unbounded and changes with units. Correlation fixes this by normalizing covariance into a fixed, comparable range. It's the number quants actually use.
Everything so far described one variable at a time. Covariance is the first tool that describes how two variables move together — the raw material of diversification, hedging, and factor models.

This distinction looks trivial and is anything but — it's the hinge the entire discipline turns on, and getting the notation right is the difference between "what I measured" and "what's actually true."
Statistics splits into two branches. Almost everything you'll ever do falls into one or the other, and confusing them is the single most common beginner mistake.

Statistics is the field that deals with the collection, organization, analysis, interpretation, and presentation of data. Every one of those steps points at a single destination: decision making. You gather data, make sense of it, and act — that's the whole arc, and if a step doesn't ultimately help someone decide something, it isn't doing its job.

Five percentiles capture the entire skeleton of a distribution — its center, its spread, and its extremes — in one compact summary. It's the basis of the box plot and of a beautifully simple, distribution-free way to flag outliers.

Central tendency and dispersion each compress a dataset to a single number. A histogram shows you the whole shape at once — it's the fastest way to see whether data is symmetric, skewed, or hiding fat tails.

Central tendency and dispersion summarize a distribution; percentiles locate a specific value within it. They're how you say "this observation is high" or "this is a bad day" precisely, without assuming any particular distribution shape.
A measure of central tendency answers the first question you ask of any dataset: where is it centered? There are three answers, and the gaps between them are as informative as the numbers themselves.

Center isn't enough. Two datasets can share the exact same mean and be completely different — one tightly clustered, one wildly spread. Dispersion measures that spread, and for a quant it's where risk lives.

Variance measures spread but leaves it in awkward squared units. Standard deviation is simply its square root — which puts the measure of spread back into the original units of the data, and that's why it's the number people actually quote.

This is a classic interview question, and there's a reason it gets asked: it tests whether you actually understand the population-vs-sample distinction or just memorized a formula. Here's the honest answer.
documents.s: Why Sample Variance Divides by n−1

documents.t: A random variable is a function that assigns a number to each outcome of a random process or experiment. The randomness lives in the process (a coin flip, a dice roll, tomorrow's market); the random variable is just the rule that turns each possible outcome into a value you can do math on.

A variable is any measurable property that can take different values from one observation to the next. Age, height, gender, price, return — each is a variable because it varies across the things you measure.
Analysis of Variance — the definition (comparing the means of two or more groups) and its two core components, factors and levels, with the medicine/dosage and mode-of-payment examples.

The four assumptions your data must satisfy before an ANOVA is valid — normality of the sampling distribution of the mean, absence of outliers, homogeneity of variance (σ₁²=σ₂²=σ₃²), and independent, random samples.

Hypothesis testing in ANOVA end to end — the F = variance-between ÷ variance-within statistic, the between vs within intuition, and a full six-step one-way ANOVA worked to F = 86.56 against the critical value 3.5546.

The three types of ANOVA — one-way (one factor, independent levels), repeated-measures (one factor, dependent levels), and factorial (two or more factors) — each with its worked example and the independent-vs-dependent distinction that separates them.
From independent vs dependent events and conditional probability to the derivation of Bayes' theorem, the base-rate trap made visual, and the link to the Naive Bayes classifier.

The chi-square goodness-of-fit test — a non-parametric test for categorical data that checks claims about population proportions by comparing an observed categorical distribution against the one a theory predicts.

The full χ² goodness-of-fit computation — a city-weights census example, worked end to end. Building the expected counts, the five steps, the right-skewed decision boundary and critical value 5.991 from the χ² table, and χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E = 26.66.
documents.s: Chi-Square for Goodness of Fit — a Worked Problem

documents.t: An orientation to inference — sampling and the standard error, confidence intervals, the classic hypothesis-testing recipe, ANOVA, the two ways to be wrong, the pitfalls of p-values, and the ROPE. The map before the module walks the territory.

What inferential statistics is, the courtroom logic of the null and alternative hypotheses, the five-step mechanism every test follows, and a worked setup — does a new college's pass rate differ from the district's 85%?
documents.s: A Hypothesis and the Hypothesis-Testing Mechanism

documents.t: The p-value defined precisely — how likely your observations are if the null were true — the significance level α, the 95% confidence region with its 0.025 tails, the coin-fairness example, and the decision rule p < α ⇒ reject.

The four outcomes of any test laid out as reality vs decision — the two correct ones and the two mistakes. Type I (false positive, rate α), Type II (false negative, rate β), statistical power, and the trade-off you can never fully escape.
documents.s: Type I and Type II Errors

documents.t: The estimation face of the same z/t machinery — a point estimate reached out by a margin of error to give a range for the unknown population mean. The formula point estimate ± z(α/2)·σ/√n, worked on the CAT-exam example to the 95% interval [480.8, 559.2].

What to do when the population σ is unknown — estimate it with the sample s and switch from the z to the t-statistic. Degrees of freedom (n − 1) explained, the fatter tails of the t, and why it converges to the normal as the sample grows.
Putting the t-distribution to work — a fully worked one-sample t-test. Does a medication change IQ? From hypotheses and degrees of freedom to the critical value ±2.045 and a t-statistic of 10.96.

The test for a mean when the population σ is known and n ≥ 30. The family of tests (z, t, chi-square, ANOVA), the z-statistic, and two fully worked examples — a two-tailed height test and a one-tailed bulb-warranty test — from hypotheses to p-value to verdict.
documents.s: Hypothesis Testing and Statistical Analysis: The Z-Test

documents.t: A single decision tree for choosing between the z-test and the t-test — driven by whether you know the population σ and whether the sample exceeds 30 — plus a side-by-side comparison.
documents.s: When to Use a t-test vs a z-test

A running log of the market blow-ups, manias and incidents worth understanding in full — what happened, the numbers, the charts, and the lesson.

A post-mortem of how Jane Street — the most profitable trading firm on Wall Street — took a ~$15B loss in July 2026, its first down month in a decade, from its 'hedge-fund side': AI-infrastructure bets, Asian equities, and a stake in the Situational Awareness fund. Why the same July storm wiped out one fund and barely dented the other.

A post-mortem of South Korea’s summer-2026 stock-market crash: how government-blessed single-stock leveraged ETFs, stacked on record margin loans and concentrated in Samsung and SK Hynix, turned a 116% boom into a 38.6% collapse — 360,000 retail accounts force-liquidated, and an emergency rewrite of the rules.

A Big Event: a coalition of state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, put Meta on trial in Oakland federal court in August 2026 — arguing Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to addict children, and that Meta knew and hid the harm. The 'Big Tobacco moment' for social media — the allegations, the internal documents, why Section 230 didn't save Meta this time, and how it ended in a $17 billion settlement.
documents.s: Meta on trial: the social-media reckoning

documents.t: A deep post-mortem of how Leopold Aschenbrenner's ~4x-levered, hyper-concentrated AI-infrastructure fund went from +439% to a 67% wipe-out in six trading days — the trigger, the positions, the failed hedges, the margin calls, and the block trade to Citadel.

A Big Event: on August 19, 2026, President Trump shared a White House podium with the CEOs of Coinbase, Ripple and Robinhood, flanked by the SEC and CFTC chairs — pushing the CLARITY Act and a regulate-by-agency pivot. Stacked with a Treasury buyback surprise, it sparked a sharp crypto rally: Bitcoin past $68,000, over $1B of shorts liquidated, Coinbase and Strategy up double digits. What a policy tailwind looks like — and why summits can also mark tops.

About Who I am​ I'm Joyeb Kashyeb — a computer science student at Jacksonville State University with a concentration in data science, deliberately building toward a career in quantitative finance. This site is my public workbench for that climb. I'm currently open to internships and roles in quantitative finance, quantitative research, and data science. If you're hiring or just want to connect, the links below reach me directly. Why I built this​ I learn by building. Reading a formula tells me almost nothing; implementing it, breaking it, and watching it respond to a slider is when it becomes mine. The rule I hold myself to across every page here: if I can't simulate or test an idea, I don't trust that I've understood it. That's why the Python runs in your browser, the pricing models have draggable inputs, and every finished topic ends with a quiz. What I'm studying right now​ Stochastic calculus — Brownian motion, Itô's lemma, and the machinery under every pricing model. Derivatives pricing — payoffs, binomial trees, Black–Scholes and the Greeks. Bayesian inference — priors, posteriors, and MCMC, headed toward probabilistic models of returns. What I've built​ Beyond the notes themselves: a browser-based Python notebook with numpy, pandas and matplotlib, a set of interactive pricing and probability labs, a live market terminal, and finance-focused coding projects like a FIFO stock ledger. The full list lives on the Projects page. Where to find me​ The full source of this site lives on GitHub. If you spot an error in any note, the "Edit this page" link at the bottom of every doc opens the GitHub editor — corrections are welcome. How rates are set, the yield curve, and their effect on markets. Einstein (allegedly) called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. Whether he said it or not, the math earns the title — a small rate difference, given enough time, becomes an enormous outcome difference: FV=P(1+rm)mtFV = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^{mt}FV=P(1+mr​)mt

LabCompound interest — the eighth wonder Starting amount $1,000 Monthly deposit $100 Annual rate 8.0% Years 20 CompoundingAnnuallyQuarterlyMonthlyDaily Final balance $64,222 You contributed $25,000 Interest earned $39,222 Growth multiple 2.57× 020,00040,00060,0000y5y10y15y20ybalancecontributionsYears The gap between the two curves is money your money made. Notice it barely exists for the first few years, then dominates — that is why quants say time in the market beats timing the market. Experiments to run: The time lever. Set 8% for 10 years, note the interest earned — now drag to 40 years. Quadrupling the time multiplies the interest by far more than 4×. Compounding is nonlinear. The rate lever. At 30 years, compare 4% vs 8%. Doubling the rate roughly quadruples the final interest. This is why the level of interest rates moves entire markets. Compounding frequency. Switch annual → daily. The gain is real but modest — frequency matters much less than rate and time. (The limit is continuous compounding, FV = Pe^rt.) Zero deposit test. Set the monthly deposit to $0 — pure compounding on the initial amount. That curve is discounting in reverse: it is exactly how bond prices relate to yields.

Discounting: every future cash flow is worth less today by exactly this math run backwards — present value = FV / (1 + r)ᵗ. All of fixed income sits on this. The yield curve plots the rate r for each maturity t. Its slope (steep, flat, inverted) is one of the most watched recession signals in macro. Policy rates (Fed, ECB, NRB) anchor the short end of the curve; expectations and term premia shape the rest.

Micro and macroeconomics, monetary vs. fiscal policy, and the economic context behind markets.

Markets don't move in a vacuum — they price expectations about growth, inflation, and policy. A quant doesn't need to be a macroeconomist, but the models don't hold without the context: interest rates set the discount factor in every valuation, central-bank policy moves the whole yield curve, and regime shifts break correlations that a backtest assumed were stable. Economics is the layer that explains why the inputs to your models change.

A forward and a future are an obligation. An option is a right, but not the obligation. Everything in this note follows from that one difference.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Call & Put Option) – Part A

documents.t: You hold an option contract to buy XYZ stock at $100, three months from now. At t=3t = 3t=3 the market can be anywhere. Two cases: Case 1 — the stock rises to $110. Your contract lets you buy at $100 while the market charges $110. You exercise: buy at 100, and you are $10 better off. Case 2 — the stock falls to $90. Your contract says $100, the market says $90. Exercising would mean paying $100 for something worth $90 — a $10 loss. So you do not execute the deal. You walk away. With a forward or a future, Case 2 is not a choice: you are obligated, and you take the $10 loss. The option gives you the flexibility to buy or not.

Buyer (holder) of the option Seller (writer / underwriter) Has The right to buy or sell — Obliged? Not obligated Always obligated to buy or sell the underlying The buyer picks whichever outcome suits them; the seller has to live with that choice. Which raises the obvious question.
documents.s: Buyer and seller are not symmetric

documents.t: Because the seller is at a structural disadvantage. They carry the obligation and have no say in whether the contract is exercised. The premium is what compensates them for taking on that obligation. It flows once, at the start, from buyer to seller: Buyer (long) ──── premium ────→ Seller (short) holds the right carries the obligation
documents.s: Why does the buyer pay a premium?

documents.t: A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying asset at the strike price KKK, on a predetermined date. You would only want a fixed price to buy at if you think the price is going up. Position What you did Expectation Long call Bought the right to buy Price will rise → bullish Short call Sold the right to buy Price will decline → bearish

A put option gives the holder the right to sell the underlying asset at KKK, on a predetermined date. Position What you did Expectation Long put Bought the right to sell Price will fall → bearish Short put Sold the right to sell Price will rise → bullish A memory aid: a bull attacks by throwing its horns up; a bear swipes down. Note the pairing is not "call = bullish". It is the combination: long call and short put are bullish; short call and long put are bearish.

Underlying asset — stocks, commodities, currencies, bonds. Strike price KKK — the price the holder can buy or sell at. Expiration date — after which the option expires worthless. Exercise style — American (exercisable at any point) or European (exercisable only at maturity). These names are conventions, not geographical locations — a European-style option is not a European product. Premium — the price paid by the holder to the seller.
documents.s: The five characteristics of an option

documents.t: This distinction matters and is easy to blur: Payoff is the value of the option at expiry, ignoring the premium. Profit is the payoff minus the premium you paid (or plus the premium you received). Payoff — premium removed: Long call = max⁡(ST−K, 0)Short call = −max⁡(ST−K, 0)Long put = max⁡(K−ST, 0)Short put = −max⁡(K−ST, 0)\begin{aligned} \text{Long call} \;&=\; \max(S_T - K,\, 0) &\qquad \text{Short call} \;&=\; -\max(S_T - K,\, 0)\\[2pt] \text{Long put} \;&=\; \max(K - S_T,\, 0) &\qquad \text{Short put} \;&=\; -\max(K - S_T,\, 0) \end{aligned}Long callLong put​=max(ST​−K,0)=max(K−ST​,0)​Short callShort put​=−max(ST​−K,0)=−max(K−ST​,0)​ Profit — what you actually walk away with: Long call = max⁡(ST−K, 0)−premiumShort call = premium−max⁡(ST−K, 0)Long put = max⁡(K−ST, 0)−premiumShort put = premium−max⁡(K−ST, 0)\begin{aligned} \text{Long call} \;&=\; \max(S_T - K,\, 0) - \text{premium}\\[2pt] \text{Short call} \;&=\; \text{premium} - \max(S_T - K,\, 0)\\[2pt] \text{Long put} \;&=\; \max(K - S_T,\, 0) - \text{premium}\\[2pt] \text{Short put} \;&=\; \text{premium} - \max(K - S_T,\, 0) \end{aligned}Long callShort callLong putShort put​=max(ST​−K,0)−premium=premium−max(ST​−K,0)=max(K−ST​,0)−premium=premium−max(K−ST​,0)​ The max(·, 0) is the option's whole character: you never exercise into a loss, so the payoff can never go below zero. Only the profit can. Everything below is profit — the version with the premium in it, since that is what determines whether the trade made money. The short is always the negative of the long — the seller's payoff is −(long payoff)-(\text{long payoff})−(long payoff). Derivatives are a zero-sum game: what one side gains, the other loses, exactly. Note also who pays and who receives: Long call and long put → pay the premium. Short call and short put → receive the premium. The short put can also be written premium+min⁡(ST−K, 0)\text{premium} + \min(S_T - K,\, 0)premium+min(ST​−K,0), which is the same thing.

Worked from the contract's side: you bought the right to sell XYZ at $100. If the market goes to $110 you do not execute — why sell at 100 what fetches 110? If it drops to $90 you do execute, gaining K - S_T = 100 - 90 = \10$.

Long calllimited loss · unlimited profitShort calllimited profit · unlimited lossLong putlimited loss · limited profitShort putlimited profit · limited lossKKKK The asymmetry is the point: Position Loss Profit Long call Limited (the premium) Unlimited — the price can keep rising Short call Unlimited Limited (the premium) Long put Limited (the premium) Limited — the price can only fall to zero Short put Limited Limited (the premium) Selling a naked call is the one position here with genuinely unbounded loss.

An option is a right, not an obligation — the holder chooses, the writer must comply. The premium exists to compensate the writer for carrying that obligation. Call = right to buy, put = right to sell; long = holds the right, short = carries the obligation and receives the premium. Bullish: long call, short put. Bearish: short call, long put. All four payoffs are built from max(·, 0), and long and short are exact negatives — a zero-sum game. Breakeven is K+premiumK + \text{premium}K+premium for a call and K−premiumK - \text{premium}K−premium for a put. Next: moneyness, and what corporate actions do to an option.

Part A covered what calls and puts are and what they pay. This note covers the two things that decide whether you would exercise at all — moneyness — and the corporate actions that quietly rewrite the contract underneath you.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Call & Put Option) – Part B

documents.t: The moneyness of an option refers to the relationship between the strike price of the option and the current price of the underlying asset. So it is a statement about the pair (ST, K)(S_T,\, K)(ST​,K), and there are only three possible relationships: ST>KST=KST<KS_T > K \qquad S_T = K \qquad S_T < KST​>KST​=KST​<K Three names follow: Term Meaning In the money (ITM) Money coming in — exercising is profitable At the money (ATM) No profit, no loss Out of the money (OTM) Money going out — exercising would lose

For a call (right to buy), you want the market above your strike: Call ITM ST>KS_T > KST​>K → profit ATM ST=KS_T = KST​=K → zero OTM ST<KS_T < KST​<K → loss For a put (right to sell), it is exactly reversed — you want the market below your strike: Put ITM ST<KS_T < KST​<K ATM ST=KS_T = KST​=K OTM ST>KS_T > KST​>K Side by side: Call Put ITM ST>KS_T > KST​>K ST<KS_T < KST​<K ATM ST=KS_T = KST​=K ST=KS_T = KST​=K OTM ST<KS_T < KST​<K ST>KS_T > KST​>K
documents.s: Which is which depends on the option

documents.t: Moneyness does not consider the premium. It is purely the intrinsic relationship between STS_TST​ and KKK. That matters, because an option can be in the money and still lose you money overall. From Part A: a long call with K=95K = 95K=95 and a premium of 1, at ST=95.5S_T = 95.5ST​=95.5, is ITM — but the payoff is 0.5−1=−0.50.5 - 1 = -0.50.5−1=−0.5. Moneyness tells you whether you would exercise; it does not tell you whether the trade was profitable. So moneyness decides one thing at expiry: whether the option is exercised or left to expire.
documents.s: One thing to be careful about

documents.t: The other half of "when can I act" is the exercise style: American — exercisable at any point during the life of the contract. Its moneyness can be checked, and acted on, all the way along. European — exercisable only at maturity. Moneyness only matters on the final date. American — exercisable at any pointEuropean — exercisable only at maturityt = 0maturity

An option contract is written on a number of shares at a strike price. A corporate action can change what a "share" even means — so the contract has to be adjusted, or the holder would be arbitrarily enriched or wiped out.

In a 3-for-1 stock split, three new shares are issued for each existing share. One XYZ share becomes three XYZ shares. The company is not worth more afterwards; the same value is just divided into more, cheaper pieces. So the option contract is adjusted to keep the holder exactly where they were. The rule: Quantity Adjustment for an nnn-for-1 split Strike price Divided by nnn → K/nK/nK/n Number of shares Multiplied by nnn

Suppose you hold a call option: Pre-split Post-split (3-for-1) Strike KKK $90 90/3=90/3 =90/3= $30 Shares per contract 100 100×3=100 \times 3 =100×3= 300 Total strike value 90×100=90 \times 100 = 90×100= $9,000 30×300=30 \times 300 = 30×300= $9,000 Identical. The split changed the units, not your position.

The same rule with n=4n = 4n=4: strike becomes K/4K/4K/4, share count becomes ×4\times 4×4. Pre-split Post-split Strike $100 $25 Shares 100 400 Total $10,000 $10,000 Again unchanged — which is the entire point of the adjustment.

A stock dividend involves a company issuing more shares to its existing stakeholders. A stock dividend is quoted as a percentage, and the trick is to convert that percentage into an equivalent split: 100%dividend % = shares you must already hold to receive one new share\frac{100\%}{\text{dividend }\%} \;=\; \text{shares you must already hold to receive one new share}dividend %100%​=shares you must already hold to receive one new share Stock dividend 100/%100/\%100/% Meaning Equivalent split 10% 10 1 new share for every 10 held 11-for-10 20% 5 1 new share for every 5 held 6-for-5 25% 4 1 new share for every 4 held 5-for-4 Once you have the equivalent split, the adjustment is the same rule as before. For a 25% stock dividend (a 5-for-4 split): shares → ×54K → ×45\text{shares} \;\to\; \times \tfrac{5}{4} \qquad\qquad K \;\to\; \times \tfrac{4}{5}shares→×45​K→×54​

Consider a put option contract to sell 100 shares of the company at $15 per share. The company then announces a 25% stock dividend. 100%/25%=4100\% / 25\% = 4100%/25%=4, so one new share for every four held — a 5-for-4 split. Pre-dividend Post-dividend Number of shares 100 100×54=100 \times \tfrac{5}{4} =100×45​= 125 Strike KKK $15 15×45=15 \times \tfrac{4}{5} =15×54​= $12 Total value 100×15=100 \times 15 =100×15= $1,500 125×12=125 \times 12 =125×12= $1,500 Unchanged, exactly as with a split.

documents.t: This one catches people out: A cash dividend does NOT adjust the option contract. If XYZ pays $3 per share in cash, the option contract is left alone. Only stock dividends and stock splits change the strike and the share count. (Cash dividends do still matter for pricing — they are an input to the Black-Scholes-Merton model — but they do not rewrite the contract terms.)

Moneyness is the relationship between STS_TST​ and KKK — ITM, ATM or OTM. For a call ITM means ST>KS_T > KST​>K; for a put it is reversed, ST<KS_T < KST​<K. Moneyness ignores the premium. It decides whether you exercise, not whether you profited. American options can be exercised any time, European only at maturity. A stock split divides the strike and multiplies the share count, leaving the contract's total value untouched. A stock dividend does the same thing, once you convert the percentage into an equivalent split via 100%/dividend %100\%/\text{dividend }\%100%/dividend % — a 25% dividend is a 5-for-4 split. A cash dividend does not adjust the contract at all.

A futures contract is marked to market daily: gains and losses are settled every single day rather than accumulating quietly until expiry. That is what stops a losing party from walking away at maturity owing more than they can pay — but it only works if there is money in the account to settle against. That money is the margin.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Operation of Margin Account)

documents.t: a) Margin account — a type of account that traders must maintain with their broker in order to engage in trading. b) Initial margin (IM) — the minimum amount of capital a trader must deposit in the margin account to open a futures position. It is usually a small percentage of the contract's total value, typically ranging from about 2% to 12%. Where in that range depends on the volatility of the asset — a more volatile underlying demands more margin. It acts as collateral, ensuring the trader can cover potential losses. c) Maintenance margin (MM) — a threshold level the margin account must maintain after the trade has been initiated. It sits below the initial margin. d) Margin call — if the account balance falls below the maintenance margin, the broker issues a margin call, and the trader must deposit additional funds to bring the account back up to the initial margin level. Variation margin is the name for that top-up: the amount of money required to restore the account to the initial margin level. Note the asymmetry that trips people up: the call is triggered by falling below MM, but the amount you must pay restores you all the way to IM — not merely back to MM.

Initial margin $12,000, maintenance margin $9,000: Balance Below MM? Margin call Day 1 $11,000 No — Day 2 $10,000 No — Day 3 $8,000 Yes Deposit $4,000 to restore $12,000 That $4,000 is the variation margin.

This is the full mechanic, day by day. A trader contacts their broker to buy two December gold futures contracts. The current futures price is $1,250 per ounce, and the contract size is 100 ounces, so the trader has contracted to buy 200 ounces at that price. Parameter Value Position Long 2 contracts = 200 oz Trade price $1,250 / oz Initial margin $6,000 per contract = $12,000 Maintenance margin $9,000 Each day the position is marked to market. Because the trader is long 200 ounces, the daily gain is daily gain=(today’s settlement−yesterday’s settlement)×200\text{daily gain} = (\text{today's settlement} - \text{yesterday's settlement}) \times 200daily gain=(today’s settlement−yesterday’s settlement)×200 Day Settlement ($/oz) Daily gain ($) Cumulative ($) Balance ($) Margin call — 1,250.00 — — 12,000 1 1,241.00 −1,800 −1,800 10,200 2 1,238.30 −540 −2,340 9,660 3 1,244.60 +1,260 −1,080 10,920 4 1,241.30 −660 −1,740 10,260 5 1,240.10 −240 −1,980 10,020 6 1,236.20 −780 −2,760 9,240 7 1,229.90 −1,260 −4,020 7,980 ← below $9,000: call for $4,020 8 1,230.80 +180 −3,840 12,180 9 1,225.40 −1,080 −4,920 11,100 10 1,228.10 +540 −4,380 11,640 11 1,211.00 −3,420 −7,800 8,220 ← below $9,000: call for $3,780 12 1,211.00 0 −7,800 12,000 13 1,214.30 +660 −7,140 12,660 14 1,216.10 +360 −6,780 13,020 15 1,223.00 +1,380 −5,400 14,400 16 1,226.90 +780 −4,620 15,180 Reading it: Day 6 ends at $9,240. Uncomfortable, but still above the $9,000 maintenance margin — no call. Day 7 the price drops to 1,229.90, a $1,260 loss, taking the balance to $7,980. That is below the maintenance margin, so the broker calls for $4,020 — the amount that restores the account to the $12,000 initial margin, not to the $9,000 threshold. Day 11 is the big one: gold falls 17.10 in a day, which on 200 ounces is a $3,420 loss. Balance $8,220 → a second call for $3,780. The position then recovers. By day 16 the balance is $15,180. Sanity check on the whole thing: the trader deposited $12,000 + $4,020 + $3,780 = $19,800 and finished with $15,180 — a net loss of $4,620, which is exactly the cumulative column, and exactly (1,226.90 − 1,250.00) × 200. The margin account never changes the economics; it only guarantees the money is there to settle them.

documents.t: Two related restrictions, both established by regulatory bodies (and so differing by country).

The maximum number of option contracts an investor or entity can hold on the same side of the market. "Same side" means positions expressing the same directional view: Side Positions Bullish long call and short put Bearish short call and long put So a long call and a short put count together against the limit — you cannot evade it by splitting a bullish bet across two instruments. With a limit of, say, 250,000 contracts, you cannot hold more than 250,000 option contracts on one side. Since one option contract is 100 shares, that is 250,000×100=25,000,000 shares250{,}000 \times 100 = 25{,}000{,}000 \text{ shares}250,000×100=25,000,000 shares Why the limit exists: to stop large entities from controlling too much of the market in a particular stock's options, and so to prevent market manipulation or liquidity problems.

Restricts the number of option contracts an investor or entity can exercise over a specific period — typically five consecutive business days. The position limit caps what you can hold; the exercise limit caps what you can act on in a window. Both close off the same abuse from different sides.

Futures are marked to market daily, and the margin account is what makes that settlement possible. Initial margin opens the position (~2–12% of contract value, driven by volatility). Maintenance margin is the lower threshold you must stay above. Fall below the MM and you get a margin call — and the variation margin you must post restores the account to the initial margin, not the threshold. On the gold example, two calls ($4,020 and $3,780) kept a position alive whose total loss was $4,620. Position limits cap contracts held on the same side of the market; exercise limits cap contracts exercised over ~5 business days. Both exist to prevent manipulation and liquidity problems.
Two worked examples, both with the numbers carried all the way through. The first uses options to reduce risk; the second uses them to magnify it. Same instrument, opposite purposes.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Practical Example on Options)

documents.t: The situation. An investor owns 1,000 shares of Company A, currently trading at $28. They are concerned about a possible share price decline over the next two months and want protection. The choice. Buy ten July put option contracts on the company's stock with a strike price of $27.50. Parameter Value Shares held 1,000 @ $28 Strike KKK $27.50 Premium $1 per share Contract size 100 shares Contracts bought 10 → covers 1,000 shares Total cost 1×100×10=1 \times 100 \times 10 =1×100×10= $1,000 The strategy costs $1,000, but guarantees the shares can be sold for at least $27.50 per share during the life of the option. That sentence is the whole idea of a hedge: you have bought a floor.

Two separate P/Ls, then the combination: Option P/L = max⁡(27.5−S, 0)×1000 − 1000Stock P/L = (S−28)×1000\begin{aligned} \text{Option P/L} \;&=\; \max(27.5 - S,\, 0) \times 1000 \;-\; 1000\\[2pt] \text{Stock P/L} \;&=\; (S - 28) \times 1000 \end{aligned}Option P/LStock P/L​=max(27.5−S,0)×1000−1000=(S−28)×1000​ Stock price SSS Option P/L ($) Stock P/L ($) Combined ($) 20 +6,500 −8,000 −1,500 21 +5,500 −7,000 −1,500 22 +4,500 −6,000 −1,500 23 +3,500 −5,000 −1,500 24 +2,500 −4,000 −1,500 25 +1,500 −3,000 −1,500 26 +500 −2,000 −1,500 27 −500 −1,000 −1,500 28 −1,000 0 −1,000 29 −1,000 +1,000 0 30 −1,000 +2,000 +1,000 32 −1,000 +4,000 +3,000 34 −1,000 +6,000 +5,000 Read the last column. Below $27.50 the combined result is frozen at −$1,500, no matter how far the stock falls. At $20 the unhedged shareholder has lost $8,000; the hedged one has lost $1,500. Above the strike the put expires worthless and the investor keeps the upside, minus the $1,000 premium. Where does −$1,500 come from? The floor is $27.50 per share, so the shares are worth at least 27.50 × 1000 = $27,500; subtract the $1,000 premium and the position is worth $26,500 against the $28,000 it started at. maximum loss = 28,000−(27.50×1000)+1,000 = $1,500\text{maximum loss} \;=\; 28{,}000 - (27.50 \times 1000) + 1{,}000 \;=\; \$1{,}500maximum loss=28,000−(27.50×1000)+1,000=$1,500 The trade-off: the investor gave up $1,000 of certain money to convert an open-ended downside into a known, capped one. On the option leg alone, breakeven is at S=26.50S = 26.50S=26.50 (where the $1 premium is exactly recovered).
documents.s: What it does, price by price

documents.t: The situation. A speculator believes a stock will increase in value over the next two months. The stock currently trades at $20. A two-month call option with a $22.50 strike is selling for $1. The speculator is willing to invest $2,000. Two ways to spend the same $2,000: Alternative What it buys A 100 shares at $20 = $2,000 B 2,000 call options (20 contracts) at $1 = $2,000

December stock price A: 100 shares B: 20 call contracts $15 (down) −$500 −$2,000 $27 (up) +$700 +$7,000 The same $2,000, the same view, and wildly different consequences. On the way up the option returns ten times what the shares do. On the way down it loses everything, while the shareholder is down only a quarter of their stake.

Option P/L = max⁡(S−22.5, 0)×2000 − 2000Stock P/L = (S−20)×100\begin{aligned} \text{Option P/L} \;&=\; \max(S - 22.5,\, 0) \times 2000 \;-\; 2000\\[2pt] \text{Stock P/L} \;&=\; (S - 20) \times 100 \end{aligned}Option P/LStock P/L​=max(S−22.5,0)×2000−2000=(S−20)×100​ SSS Option P/L ($) Stock P/L ($) 15.5 −2,000 −450 16.5 −2,000 −350 17.5 −2,000 −250 18.5 −2,000 −150 19.5 −2,000 −50 20.5 −2,000 +50 21.5 −2,000 +150 22.5 −2,000 +250 23.5 0 +350 24.5 +2,000 +450 25.5 +4,000 +550 26.5 +6,000 +650 27.5 +8,000 +750 Note the shape. The option line is flat at −$2,000 for every price below the $22.50 strike — the speculator is wiped out identically whether the stock ends at 15.5 or 22.5. Then it turns and climbs at 2,000 per dollar, twenty times the slope of the share position. Breakeven is at S=K+premium=22.50+1=$23.50S = K + \text{premium} = 22.50 + 1 = \$23.50S=K+premium=22.50+1=$23.50 which is where the option column crosses zero.

Leverage the position with options. The option gives exposure to 2,000 shares for the price of 100. That is the leverage: a large exposure for a small outlay. It amplifies the return — and amplifies the loss in exactly the same proportion. The shareholder needs the stock to fall to zero to lose everything; the option holder only needs it to finish a cent below $22.50.

The same instrument hedges or speculates depending on how it is used against the position you already hold. A protective put buys a floor: the 1,000-share holder converted an $8,000 loss at $20 into a capped $1,500, at a cost of $1,000, while keeping the upside. A long call used for speculation gives leverage: $2,000 controlled 2,000 shares instead of 100, turning a $700 gain into $7,000 — and a $500 loss into a total $2,000 loss. Breakeven in both cases is the strike adjusted by the premium: K−PK - PK−P for the put leg, K+PK + PK+P for the call.

The Greeks are risk measures used in options to assess the sensitivity of the option price to various factors. An option's price does not depend on one thing. It moves with the underlying asset, with time, with interest rates, and with volatility. Each Greek isolates one of those and asks: if this input moves, how much does the option price move? There are five: Greek Sensitivity of the option price with respect to… Delta (Δ\DeltaΔ) the underlying asset Gamma (Γ\GammaΓ) (the sensitivity of delta to the underlying asset) Theta (Θ\ThetaΘ) time Rho (ρ\rhoρ) the risk-free rate Vega implied volatility Gamma is the odd one out: it is a sensitivity of another Greek, not of the price directly.

Delta tells the sensitivity of the option price with respect to the underlying asset — or equivalently, the rate of change of the option price relative to the change in the underlying asset. Δ=∂V∂S\Delta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}Δ=∂S∂V​ where VVV is the price of the option and SSS is the price of the underlying asset. So ∂V\partial V∂V is the change in the option price and ∂S\partial S∂S the change in the underlying asset price.

Because the option price is a function of several variables at once — the asset price, volatility, the rate, time. A function of one variable gives an ordinary derivative (an ODE, dV/dSdV/dSdV/dS); a function of many gives a partial derivative (a PDE, ∂V/∂S\partial V / \partial S∂V/∂S), which holds everything else fixed and varies only SSS. Option pricing is the second case.

Delta can be positive or negative, and which one depends on the type of option and the position you hold. Positive delta — a positive relationship with the underlying: the option value rises when the stock price rises the option value falls when the stock price falls Negative delta — a negative relationship: the option price falls when the underlying rises the option price rises when the underlying falls A put has negative delta for exactly this reason: you hold the right to sell, so a rising stock makes that right less valuable.

Call option: 0 to 1Put option: 0 to −1\text{Call option: } 0 \text{ to } 1 \qquad\qquad \text{Put option: } 0 \text{ to } -1Call option: 0 to 1Put option: 0 to −1 Taking the position into account as well: Position Delta range Long call 0 to +1 Short call 0 to −1 Long put 0 to −1 Short put 0 to +1 Laid on a number line, −1 is where long put and short call live; +1 is where long call and short put live.
documents.s: Range, by option and by position

documents.t: Suppose the delta of a call is 0.5. Then Δ=∂V∂S=∂V1=0.5 ⟹ ∂V=$0.5\Delta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial V}{1} = 0.5 \;\Longrightarrow\; \partial V = \$0.5Δ=∂S∂V​=1∂V​=0.5⟹∂V=$0.5 For every $1 increase in the underlying asset, the option price increases by $0.50. And for a put with delta −0.5: a $1 rise in the asset makes the put price fall by $0.50. These values come out of the option pricing models — Black-Scholes, the binomial tree, or Monte Carlo. Delta is not assumed; it is computed.

For a call: Moneyness Delta ITM 0.5 to 1 ATM ≈ 0.5 OTM 0 to 0.5 For a put, mirrored into the negatives: Moneyness Delta ITM −0.5 to −1 ATM ≈ −0.5 OTM 0 to −0.5 This is standard practice among traders and risk managers for defining moneyness — rather than comparing SSS and KKK directly, they read it off the delta.

This is the interpretation worth carrying around: Delta is the probability of the option contract being in the money at expiry. Δ=0.2\Delta = 0.2Δ=0.2 → roughly a 20% chance of finishing in the money — clearly OTM territory. Δ=0.5\Delta = 0.5Δ=0.5 → a coin flip — at the money. Δ\DeltaΔ between 0.5 and 1 → a 50% to 100% chance — in the money. Δ=1\Delta = 1Δ=1 → effectively certain. And recall what each outcome means at expiry: ITM you receive money, ATM no profit and no loss, OTM you have paid the money (the premium) for nothing.

Take an OTM call. With a long time to maturity, the stock has more time to move up to the strike, so there is a higher chance of expiring ITM — and therefore a higher delta. Two days from expiry, the stock has almost no room to travel, the probability collapses, and delta with it. Long-term maturity⇒higher deltaShort-term maturity⇒lower delta\text{Long-term maturity} \Rightarrow \text{higher delta} \qquad \text{Short-term maturity} \Rightarrow \text{lower delta}Long-term maturity⇒higher deltaShort-term maturity⇒lower delta

The same logic through a different lever. High volatility — the stock moves around more, so an OTM option has a higher probability of expiring ITM → higher delta. Low volatility — fluctuation is small, the probability of reaching the strike is low → lower delta. Both effects are really one effect: anything that raises the chance of finishing in the money raises delta, because delta is that chance.

The Greeks are risk measures: the sensitivity of the option price to each input. Five of them — delta, gamma, theta, rho, vega. Δ=∂V/∂S\Delta = \partial V/\partial SΔ=∂V/∂S — a partial derivative, because the option price depends on several variables at once. Call delta runs 0 to +1, put delta 0 to −1; the short of each flips the sign. A delta of 0.5 means a $1 move in the underlying moves the option $0.50. Delta is the probability of finishing in the money — which is why traders use it to define moneyness (ITM 0.5–1, ATM ≈0.5, OTM 0–0.5 for a call). More time → higher delta. More volatility → higher delta. Both raise the chance of expiring ITM.
Delta answers "how much does the option move when the stock moves?" But delta itself is not constant — it changes as the stock moves. Gamma measures that.

Gamma tells how sensitive your delta is with respect to the change in the underlying asset. Γ=∂Δ∂S=∂2V∂S2\Gamma = \frac{\partial \Delta}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}Γ=∂S∂Δ​=∂S2∂2V​ Since delta is already the first derivative of the option price, gamma is the second derivative — the curvature of the option's price curve. Consequence Gamma is higher Delta is more sensitive to the underlying — when the stock fluctuates, delta changes rapidly Gamma is lower Delta is less sensitive — delta adjusts slowly, even if the stock price moves a lot Read geometrically, ∂Δ/∂S\partial \Delta / \partial S∂Δ/∂S is the slope of the delta curve. Where the delta curve is steep, gamma is high; where it is flat, gamma is near zero.

This is the shape to remember. Delta traces an S-curve against the stock price; its slope — gamma — is therefore a bell, peaking exactly where the delta curve is steepest: Delta (call)SATMGammaSATMhighestOTMITM Gamma is highest at ATM. Gamma is lowest at ITM and OTM — at both extremes the delta curve flattens out (delta is pinned near 0 or near ±1), so it has almost no slope left to give. And note: the gamma curve is the same for a call and a put. The delta curves are different (0 to 1 versus 0 to −1) but they have the same slope at every stock price, and gamma is that slope.

Gamma is always positive — for both call options and put options. This trips people up, because delta's sign depends on call versus put. Gamma's does not: buying either a call or a put buys curvature. What does differ is who benefits.

Long call. As the underlying price rises, the delta rises (say 0.5 → 0.7), so the option becomes more sensitive to price changes in the direction you want. A $1 rise now earns $0.70 instead of $0.50. Positive gamma benefits the long position. Short call. Gamma is still positive, but your exposure is negative. As the underlying rises, the delta of the short call moves further negative (−0.5 → −0.7) — so each additional $1 rise costs you $0.70 instead of $0.50. The position loses money at an accelerating rate. Long position⇒gamma favours youShort position⇒gamma works against you\text{Long position} \Rightarrow \text{gamma favours you} \qquad \text{Short position} \Rightarrow \text{gamma works against you}Long position⇒gamma favours youShort position⇒gamma works against you That asymmetry is the reason short option positions are dangerous in a fast market: the loss rate itself increases as the move continues.

Here is the part that surprises people, because it runs opposite to delta: Maturity Gamma Effect on delta Short-term Higher gamma Delta changes pretty fast Long-term Lower gamma Delta changes slowly over time Intuitively: near expiry, an at-the-money option is on a knife edge — a small move in the stock flips it from "probably worthless" to "probably exercised", so its delta swings violently from near 0 to near 1. That violent swing is high gamma. A long-dated option has time to absorb the same move, so its delta barely reacts. Compare with Part A: more time raises delta but lowers gamma.

Γ=change in deltachange in the asset=∂2V∂S2\Gamma = \dfrac{\text{change in delta}}{\text{change in the asset}} = \dfrac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}Γ=change in the assetchange in delta​=∂S2∂2V​ — the second derivative, the curvature. Gamma is always positive, for calls and puts alike, and the gamma curve is the same for both. Highest at ATM; lowest at ITM and OTM — a bell, because it is the slope of delta's S-curve. Gamma favours the long position and works against the short, because the short's losses accelerate. Short-dated options have high gamma; long-dated have low gamma — the reverse of delta's relationship with time.
Delta and gamma are about the stock moving. Theta is about nothing happening at all — the option losing value simply because a day went by.

Theta measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to time. It represents how much the price of an option falls as time passes (each day). Θ=∂V∂t=change in option pricechange in time\Theta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial t} = \frac{\text{change in option price}}{\text{change in time}}Θ=∂t∂V​=change in timechange in option price​ Theta is also called time decay, because an option loses its value as we approach maturity. An option contract bought at t=0t=0t=0 and expiring at t=3t=3t=3 months is, all else equal, worth a little less every single day of that journey. Formally: it tells how much the price of the option will decrease as each day passes, holding all other factors constant.

You own a call option: Current stock price $100 Strike price $100 Time to expiry 30 days Theta −$0.10 per day As every day passes, the value of your option decreases by $0.10. If theta is negative, the option price declines by that much. If theta is positive, the option price increases by that much.

This is the part that matters in practice. Theta is negative for a LONG position — long call and long put. When you are the buyer, theta works against you. Think of an ice cube. As time passes, does the ice cube melt? Yes. Time is working against the ice cube — and against you. Theta is positive for a SHORT position — short call and short put. As time passes, the short position benefits from time decay. Think of renting out a house. You collect rent from the person staying there. The more days they stay, the more rent they pay. Time is working in support of you. Long⇒Θ<0 (against you)Short⇒Θ>0 (in your favour)\text{Long} \Rightarrow \Theta < 0 \text{ (against you)} \qquad \text{Short} \Rightarrow \Theta > 0 \text{ (in your favour)}Long⇒Θ<0 (against you)Short⇒Θ>0 (in your favour) This is the mirror image of gamma, which favours the long. The option seller collects decay but carries accelerating directional risk; the buyer pays decay for that convexity. That trade-off is the heart of option trading.
Time decay is not linear. It is slow while the option is young and accelerates sharply into the final days: OptionvalueDays to expiration9060200decay is slow while there is time……then collapses

Theta only makes sense once the option price is split in two. Intrinsic value — the real value of the option if exercised right now: Call: ST−KPut: K−ST\text{Call: } S_T - K \qquad\qquad \text{Put: } K - S_TCall: ST​−KPut: K−ST​ If that is negative the option would not be exercised, so OTM intrinsic value is 0. (With K=100K=100K=100 and the stock at 110, a call's intrinsic value is 10.) Extrinsic value — also called time value: The additional value beyond the intrinsic value, which accounts for factors such as time to expiration and volatility. Putting them together: Option price=Intrinsic value+Extrinsic value\text{Option price} = \text{Intrinsic value} + \text{Extrinsic value}Option price=Intrinsic value+Extrinsic value Theta eats the extrinsic value only. Intrinsic value is untouched by the calendar — it is arithmetic on today's prices. So an option's exposure to time decay is exactly its exposure to extrinsic value.
Everything follows from that last sentence.

ITM options have a significant amount of intrinsic value, so the price is less dependent on time decay. As expiration approaches, the intrinsic value dominates and the extrinsic value becomes smaller and smaller — so theta is smaller.

Here ST=KS_T = KST​=K, so the intrinsic value is exactly zero and the option price is extrinsic value only. It is pure time value — and there is more of it here than anywhere else. Theta is highest for ATM options. They have the greatest potential to lose value as time passes.

Intrinsic value is zero as well, but the extrinsic value is small. Worked through — an OTM call with K=110K = 110K=110 while the stock sits at S=100S = 100S=100: Case 1 — 30 days to expiry There is still a real chance the stock climbs to 110, so the option still has some time value. Decay is relatively slow. Case 2 — 5 days to expiry In a normal market it is highly unlikely the stock travels from 100 to 110. Intrinsic value is zero and the remaining extrinsic value evaporates → theta is high, and decay accelerates in the final days. So the conclusion is two-sided, and both halves matter: Theta decay is relatively slower for an OTM option at longer maturity… …but as expiration approaches, the chance of becoming ITM diminishes and theta accelerates — the option loses its value much faster.

Θ=∂V/∂t\Theta = \partial V / \partial tΘ=∂V/∂t — the option's daily bleed, all else equal. A theta of −$0.10 costs you ten cents a day. Long → theta negative, time against you (the melting ice cube). Short → theta positive, time for you (collecting rent). Option price = intrinsic + extrinsic, and theta only consumes the extrinsic part. Theta is highest ATM (pure time value), lower ITM and OTM. Decay is convex — slow early, accelerating hard into the last days.
Delta and gamma track the stock. Theta tracks the calendar. Vega tracks uncertainty itself.

Vega measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to implied volatility — how much the price of the option will change for a 1% change in the implied volatility of the asset. V=∂V∂σ\mathcal{V} = \frac{\partial V}{\partial \sigma}V=∂σ∂V​ where VVV is the option price and σ\sigmaσ the volatility, so ∂σ\partial \sigma∂σ is the change in volatility.

The distinction is simply which direction in time you are looking: Historical volatility Volatility of the past — what the asset actually did Implied volatility Volatility of the future — what the market currently expects Vega is about the implied one. Historical volatility is measured; implied volatility is a market expectation baked into today's option prices, and it can sit above or below the historical figure. Volatility itself gets modelled two broad ways: Family Models Time-series models ARCH, GARCH, EWMA (and the wider AR, MA, ARIMA, ARIMAX, SARIMA, VAR family) Stochastic-volatility models Heston, SABR, the 3/2 model

A call option: Stock price $100 Strike $100 Time to expiry 30 days Vega 0.15 For every 1% increase in implied volatility, the option price will increase by $0.15. Meaning High vega The option price is very sensitive to volatility — a small increase in volatility raises the option price significantly Low vega Changes in volatility have only a small impact on the price

Vega is always non-negative. Rising volatility always raises an option's value — call or put, in or out of the money. The reason is the payoff's asymmetry, and it is worth doing properly because it explains the entire Greek.

A long call pays max⁡(ST−K, 0)\max(S_T - K,\, 0)max(ST​−K,0), with K=100K = 100K=100. Suppose higher volatility means the stock could land at 120 or 80 instead of staying near 100: Outcome Payoff ST=120S_T = 120ST​=120 max⁡(120−100, 0)=20\max(120 - 100,\, 0) = \mathbf{20}max(120−100,0)=20 ST=80S_T = 80ST​=80 max⁡(80−100, 0)=0\max(80 - 100,\, 0) = \mathbf{0}max(80−100,0)=0 Up, you exercise and profit. Down, you simply do not exercise — no profit, no loss beyond the premium already paid. The upside is open-ended; the downside is floored at zero. More volatility therefore adds only upside.
documents.s: Why volatility helps the long — a call

documents.t: A long put pays max⁡(K−ST, 0)\max(K - S_T,\, 0)max(K−ST​,0), same K=100K = 100K=100: Outcome Payoff ST=120S_T = 120ST​=120 max⁡(100−120, 0)=0\max(100 - 120,\, 0) = \mathbf{0}max(100−120,0)=0 ST=80S_T = 80ST​=80 max⁡(100−80, 0)=20\max(100 - 80,\, 0) = \mathbf{20}max(100−80,0)=20 Identical logic, mirrored. Which gives the rule: Long position (call or put)⇒vega is your friend\text{Long position (call or put)} \Rightarrow \text{vega is your friend}Long position (call or put)⇒vega is your friendShort position⇒vega works against you\text{Short position} \Rightarrow \text{vega works against you}Short position⇒vega works against you The short side wrote that floored payoff, so every increase in volatility hands value to the buyer at the seller's expense.

Moneyness Vega ATM Highest ITM Low OTM Low Why ATM. At the money, ST=KS_T = KST​=K — the option sits exactly on the knife edge. Even a small change in volatility can tip it either way: to 101 and it is ITM, to 99 and it is OTM. That balance is where extra uncertainty is worth the most. Why not ITM. A deep in-the-money option is already going to be exercised; its value is mostly intrinsic. More volatility barely moves that, so the impact on the option price is small. Why not OTM. Far out of the money, the option is unlikely to be exercised regardless, so extra volatility changes little. Note this is the same bell shape as gamma — both peak at the money, for the same underlying reason: that is where the option's fate is least decided.

Maturity Vega Long-term (e.g. 3 months) High Short-term (e.g. 5 days) Low Short duration means the stock has less room to travel, so the option price is less impacted by a change in volatility. Think of bouncing a ball. Dropped from high up it bounces high — that is high vega. Held near the floor and released, it barely bounces — low vega. Volatility needs room, and room is time.

Worth holding the four together, because their behaviour with time diverges: More time to expiry Peak at Delta Higher — (monotonic S-curve) Gamma Lower ATM Theta Lower per day (until it accelerates near expiry) ATM Vega Higher ATM Gamma and vega share the ATM peak but move in opposite directions with time: a short-dated ATM option is a gamma instrument, a long-dated ATM option is a vega instrument.
documents.s: How vega compares with the others

documents.t: V=∂V/∂σ\mathcal{V} = \partial V / \partial \sigmaV=∂V/∂σ — the price change per 1% move in implied volatility. Vega 0.15 means +$0.15 per point of IV. Implied volatility is the market's view of the future; historical is the measured past. Vega is always non-negative, because the option payoff is floored at zero: volatility adds upside without adding downside. Long is long vega (calls and puts alike); short is short vega. Vega is highest ATM — the knife edge — and low both ITM and OTM. Long-dated options carry high vega; short-dated carry little — the bouncing ball needs height.
The last of the five, and the one traders think about least — until rates start moving.

Rho measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to the risk-free interest rate — the change in price for a 1% change in that rate. ρ=∂V∂r\rho = \frac{\partial V}{\partial r}ρ=∂r∂V​ where rrr is the risk-free rate.

The theoretical return on an investment with no risk. In practice it is the US Treasury rate (or SOFR). The mechanism is simple: the US government issues bonds to acquire money, people lend to it because it is considered as close to riskless as exists, and the return on that lending is the risk-free interest rate.

Option Rho Meaning Call +0.05 For every 1% increase in the interest rate, the option price increases by $0.05 Put −0.04 For every 1% increase in the risk-free rate, the put price decreases by $0.04 So immediately: Call⇒ρ>0Put⇒ρ<0\text{Call} \Rightarrow \rho > 0 \qquad\qquad \text{Put} \Rightarrow \rho < 0Call⇒ρ>0Put⇒ρ<0

This is the one Greek whose sign is best understood through present value. When the interest rate rises, the present value of the strike price falls. Discounting means the interest rate and the discounted amount are inversely related — a $110 strike payable in three months might be worth only $100 in today's money once rates rise. Now split by option type, asking who pays the strike: Call — you PAY the strike. A call holder will hand over KKK to buy the stock. If the present value of that obligation falls, you are effectively paying less. Rising rates worked in your favour → rho is positive. Put — you RECEIVE the strike. A put holder sells the stock and collects KKK. If the present value of what you will receive falls, you are collecting a lesser price in today's terms. Rising rates work against you → rho is negative.

Maturity Rho Why Short-term (5 days) Low The interest rate has little chance to fluctuate in five days, so the option price will not fluctuate either Long-term (60 days+) High Rates can move a lot over that horizon, so the impact on the option price is significant Rho therefore grows with maturity — the same direction as vega and delta, the opposite of gamma.

Here rho breaks the pattern of the other Greeks. Gamma, vega and theta all peak at the money. Rho does not — it is monotonic, and highest in the money: Call option Put option ITM Highest +ve rho Highest −ve rho ATM Moderate +ve rho Moderate −ve rho OTM Lowest +ve rho Lowest −ve rho Why ITM is highest. An in-the-money option is dominated by its intrinsic value (ST−KS_T - KST​−K), with the extrinsic part small. That intrinsic value contains KKK — and KKK is exactly the term discounting acts on. So the option is impacted a lot by the interest rate → higher rho. Why OTM is lowest. An out-of-the-money option has no intrinsic value at all; it is pure extrinsic value. There is no strike payment in the money to discount, so the rate barely touches it → lower rho.

Rho becomes extremely important when interest rates are expected to rise or fall. Conversely, in a stable interest-rate environment rho becomes less significant, and delta, gamma, theta and vega dominate the risk picture. That is why rho is the Greek most often ignored — and why ignoring it stops being safe the moment a central bank starts moving.

With rho done, the full set: Greek Measures sensitivity to Sign Peaks at With more time Delta Δ\DeltaΔ Underlying price Call +, put − — (S-curve) Higher Gamma Γ\GammaΓ Delta (2nd derivative) Always + ATM Lower Theta Θ\ThetaΘ Time Long −, short + ATM Lower per day Vega V\mathcal{V}V Implied volatility Always ≥ 0 ATM Higher Rho ρ\rhoρ Risk-free rate Call +, put − ITM Higher Two patterns worth carrying away: Gamma, theta and vega all peak at the money — that is where an option's fate is least decided, so that is where uncertainty is worth most. Rho is the exception, peaking in the money, because it acts on the strike rather than on uncertainty. Long positions are long gamma and long vega but short theta. You pay decay every day in exchange for convexity and volatility exposure. The short side takes the opposite trade. That single sentence is most of option trading.

documents.t: ρ=∂V/∂r\rho = \partial V / \partial rρ=∂V/∂r — the price change per 1% move in the risk-free rate (US Treasury / SOFR). Calls have positive rho, puts negative — because rising rates cut the present value of the strike, which helps the buyer who pays it and hurts the buyer who receives it. Longer-dated options have more rho; short-dated have almost none. Rho is highest ITM, not ATM — it tracks the strike, and the strike matters most where intrinsic value dominates. It matters when rates are expected to move, and is largely ignorable when they are not.

documents.t: Quant Finance Bootcamp: Derivatives, Risk Management & Quant Modeling What will I learn as a student from here? Foundational Knowledge: Gain a solid understanding of derivative markets, including forwards, futures, and options, and the roles of different traders like hedgers, arbitrageurs, and speculators. Future Markets: Learn the intricacies of futures contracts, margin account operations, and the distinctions between forward and future contracts through case studies. Options Mechanics: Master the types of options, positions, and payoff diagrams, and differentiate between European and American options. Option Pricing: Explore the binomial tree method for pricing American options and the concept of risk-neutral valuation. Stochastic Processes: Delve into continuous and discrete stochastic processes, Brownian motion, and apply Ito's Lemma to quantitative finance models. Black-Scholes Model: Understand the assumptions, application, and interpretation of the Black-Scholes Merton model for option pricing. Risk Management with Greeks: Learn how to calculate and use Delta, Gamma, Rho, Theta, and Vega for hedging and risk management. Value at Risk (VaR): Analyze risk using VaR and Expected Shortfall, with backtesting and stress testing to validate models. Exotic Options: Explore the unique characteristics and applications of exotic options such as Asian, binary, and barrier options. Interest Rate Modeling: Study stochastic interest rate models like Vasicek and CIR, focusing on their calibration, implementation, and differences.

The Capital Asset Pricing Model and the theory of risk and return. CAPM's one-line claim: you only get paid for the risk you can't diversify away. FlashcardsCAPM vocabulary term Beta (β) tap to reveal definition Sensitivity of an asset’s return to the market’s return: β = Cov(Rᵢ, Rₘ) / Var(Rₘ). β = 1 moves with the market, β > 1 amplifies it, β < 1 dampens it, β < 0 hedges it. ← Prev1 / 7Next →🔀 Shuffle

A stock has β = 1.4. With a risk-free rate of 3% and an expected market return of 8%: E[R]=3%+1.4×(8%−3%)=10%E[R] = 3\% + 1.4 \times (8\% - 3\%) = 10\%E[R]=3%+1.4×(8%−3%)=10% If your research says the stock will actually return 13%, CAPM says it offers +3% alpha — either you've found a bargain, or your forecast (or CAPM itself) is wrong. Quant careers are built on telling those two apart.

Forwards, futures, options, and swaps — the core derivative instruments and how they are priced and used. A derivative is a contract whose value derives from something else (a stock, an index, a rate). The fastest way to build intuition is to play with payoffs — so play:

Pick a strategy, drag the strike and premium, and watch how the profit/loss profile changes. Green is where you make money at expiry, red is where you lose it. Short Put — this is how "picking up pennies in front of a steamroller" looks: small capped profit, big downside. Long Straddle — you don't care about direction, only movement. Both tails are green.
